rv.q: That’s clearly the balance Chinese Republicans wants to strike as a whole, but even as Iris stands surefooted, the play itself is still teetering.
For a satire, “Chinese Republicans” is told disappointingly straight.
Chinese Republicans is tense, sharp, and barkingly funny.
While the structure of the play is too schematic, Chay Yew’s production moves fast enough to be a comedy, as well as a trenchant drama with an unforeseen ending.
Above all, Yew’s excellent ensemble makes the most out of Lin’s cutting dialogue.
Much of “Chinese Republicans” provides a deepening and ultimately poignant portrait of four distinct characters, made all the more palpable by a first-rate cast.
The longer the piece goes on, the less sure you may feel you understand what Lin is truly writing about!
If Chinese Republicans contains the occasional dramatic infelicity, it also presents a playwright we'll want to hear more from.
The play is an intriguing microcosm of yet another aspect of unchecked bigotry.
What it doesn’t add up to, alas, is a compelling piece of theatre.
Chinese Republicans does it all— leading with laughter and pushing boundaries with both kindness and dignity.
Delightful and a bit spicy, Chinese Republicans is the kind of lunch you actually want to linger over...
Instead, she’s written a smart, sharp play that shows us women in the workplace, fighting the good fight and not always winning.

Chinese Republicans may occasionally overreach in its ambitions, but it is still a fun ride that brings up thorny issues you will want to discuss over Chinatown turnip cakes or even croissants at Paris Baguette.
What makes Chinese Republicans stand out is its willingness to sit inside contradiction.

Lin’s script contains well-observed character beats and moments of subtlety, as well as witty bons mots and subversive surprises, but the tendency for each character to express her feelings in expository speech suggests a lack of trust in the audience.
But in “Chinese Republicans,” she hasn’t yet found the dramatic crucible to forge them together.
When Chinese Republicans trusts its characters, it's electric. When it doesn't, even the Louboutins can't carry it.
This late-stage awakening to the downsides of late-stage capitalism doesn’t feel authentic.
Except for the names, faces and accents, Chinese Republicans doesn’t offer anything we haven’t seen before.
But important themes don’t automatically make important drama.
There is something very disingenuous to a story about Republicans—first- and second-generation immigrants, no less—who have nothing to say about Trump.

cn.t: Critics find Lin's corporate satire promising but uneven, praising sharp dialogue and strong performances while faulting a muddled script that struggles to balance its many ambitious themes about identity, power, and assimilation.

vr.q: Chinese republicans is the kind of play that immediately sparks conversation.
I do still think this play is worth seeing
This play frustrated me because I really wanted to like it, but I don't think it's there yet.
